title: Market Cap: The Only Size That Matters

cards.headline: A $500 stock is not expensive.
cards.body: Price per share tells you what one slice costs. It tells you nothing about the size of the pie. To know how big a company is, you need a second number: how many slices exist.

art.name: price-vs-value
art.alt: A five-hundred-dollar share price shown as different from the value of the whole business.

cards.headline: Market cap is price times share count.
cards.body: Nimbus trades at $5 with 12 billion shares outstanding: that is a **$60 billion** company. Cobalt trades at $500 with 30 million shares: **$15 billion**. The five-dollar stock is the business four times bigger.

art.name: market-cap-equation
art.alt: Share price multiplied by shares outstanding equals market capitalization.

cards.title: Same price gap, opposite size gap
cards.caption: Nimbus costs $5 a share, Cobalt costs $500. The cheaper-looking stock belongs to the company worth four times as much.

cards.prompt: One stock trades at $8. Another trades at $900. Which company is worth more?

options.label: You cannot tell from price alone

cards.explanation: Price is one of two factors. Without the share count you know only what a single slice costs. Multiply price by shares outstanding, then compare.

cards.headline: Cheap-looking is not cheap.
cards.body: A $3 stock feels like more upside than a $300 stock because you can buy a hundred of them. But $300 buys $300 of the business either way. How many slices a company cut itself into is arbitrary.

art.name: price-vs-value
art.alt: A low-looking share price contrasted with the value of the whole business.

cards.body: So investors sort companies by market cap, never by share price. Three rough buckets do most of the work.

cards.headline: The bands are conventions, not rules.
cards.body: No regulator defines large cap. Index providers and fund managers each draw the lines differently, and the lines drift upward as markets grow. Treat the buckets as shorthand for size, not as an official category.

art.name: size-spectrum
art.alt: Small-, mid-, and large-cap company bands arranged as an increasing size spectrum.

cards.body: A 10-for-1 stock split hands you ten times as many shares at one tenth the price. The company's market cap is [[1]].
cards.explanation: A split re-slices the pie without changing its size. Nothing about the business moved, so nothing about its value did either. A reverse split works the same way, backwards.

cards.summary: Share price is half an equation. Market cap, price times shares outstanding, is the number that tells you how big a company actually is.
bullets: Market cap equals share price multiplied by shares outstanding.
A $5 stock can be a far bigger company than a $500 stock.
Size buckets are useful shorthand, but the boundaries are conventions.
A split changes the price and the share count, never the market cap.

cards.insight: Price tells you what one slice costs. Only market cap tells you how big the pie is.
